title: The Future
summary: The simplest tense in the language: one marker, **-s-**, inserted between the stem and the ending, and one set of endings for every verb there is. The only difficulty is what happens when the stem already ends in a consonant that will not stand beside an s.

rules.heading: The Future Formed with -s-
rules.statement: The future is built from the **infinitive** stem — the infinitive less its *-ti* — with **-s-** and the endings below. There is no division into conjugations here and no second stem to learn: whatever a verb does in the present and the past, its future is regular.

paradigms.caption: dirbti → the future
paradigms.footnote: The third person is the bare stem with *-s* and nothing after it, and it serves both numbers as in the other tenses (¶57).

examples.gloss: Tomorrow I shall read a book.

rules.heading: Consonant Changes before the -s-
rules.statement: Where the infinitive stem already ends in **s, z, š, ž**, the marker cannot be heard beside it and the two merge into one consonant. Where it ends in **d** or **t**, that consonant becomes **s**. The endings are untouched; only the joint is affected, and the change is one of pronunciation written down rather than a grammatical irregularity.

paradigms.caption: Stems that alter
paradigms.footnote: Verbs whose stem ends in a vowel — *skaity-*, *kalbė-*, *važiuo-* — never alter: *skaitysiu*, *kalbėsiu*, *važiuosiu*.

rules.heading: The Future of Būti
rules.statement: **Būti** follows the rule exactly, and its third person **bus** is among the most useful words in the language: it does duty for *there will be*, *it will be*, and *they will be* together, and it is what a Lithuanian says when asked whether something is going to happen.

examples.gloss: Tomorrow I shall be at home.

examples.note: genitive after an existential question, as with *yra* and *nėra*

rules.heading: Negation in the Future
rules.statement: As in the other tenses, **ne-** is written onto the front of the verb and the object of the negated verb passes into the **genitive**. Nothing new is needed; what is needed is the habit, since a learner who has mastered the genitive of negation in the present often loses it the moment the tense changes.

examples.gloss: I shall not buy this book.

rules.heading: Saying What Will Happen
rules.statement: The future serves for intention, for promise and for prediction alike; Lithuanian has no separate *going to*. Its usual markers are **rytoj** (tomorrow), **kitą savaitę** (next week) and **po** with the genitive (¶33). Note that where English uses a present tense after *when* and *if* in speaking of the future, Lithuanian uses the **future** there too, and says what it means.

paradigms.caption: Where English changes tense and Lithuanian does not

rows.label: after when
cells: When I get back, I'll ring.

examples.gloss: Next week we shall go to the seaside.
In a month he will be in Lithuania.

drills.stem: What is the future first person singular of **dirbti**?
drills.explanation: Stem *dirb-* plus the marker **-s-** plus the ending **-iu**: *dirbsiu*. *dirbs* is the third person.

drills.stem: Complete: **Rytoj ____ namie.** (Tomorrow I shall be at home.)
drills.explanation: *būti* is regular in the future: *būsiu*. *bus* would be the third person — *he will be*, or *there will be*.

drills.stem: What is the future third person of **skaityti**?
drills.explanation: The stem *skaity-* ends in a vowel, so nothing alters: *skaity-* + *-s* gives **skaitys**, serving both singular and plural.

drills.stem: Why is the future of **grįžti** *grįšiu* and not *grįžsiu*?
options: Because *grįžti* is irregular and must be memorised.
Because a stem ending in ž merges with the -s- marker into a single š.
Because the first person always drops a consonant.
drills.explanation: Stems in **s, z, š, ž** absorb the marker; *grįž-* + *-s-* gives *grįš-*. It is a change of sound written down, not an irregularity: the endings are the ordinary ones.

drills.stem: In which of these does the stem **change** before the -s- of the future?
drills.explanation: *ved-* becomes *ves-* (d → s) and *neš-* absorbs the marker to give *neš-*. *dirb-* ends in b and *kalbė-* in a vowel, so both are untouched: *dirbsiu*, *kalbėsiu*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš nepirksiu šios ____.** (I shall not buy this book.)
drills.explanation: A negated verb puts its object in the genitive, in the future as in every other tense: *knygos*. The demonstrative *šios* is in the genitive with it.

drills.stem: **Kai grįšiu, skambinsiu.** Why is the first verb in the future and not the present?
options: Because Lithuanian puts a future meaning into the future tense in both halves, where English uses a present after *when*.
Because the two verbs must always match in tense.
drills.explanation: English says *when I get back* with a present; Lithuanian says what it means and uses the future. *kai* governs nothing — it merely joins.

drills.stem: Which of these are correctly formed futures?
drills.explanation: *grįžsi* is wrong: the ž absorbs the marker, giving **grįši**. The other three are regular — a vowel stem, a t → s stem, and *būti*.

options: Because the question asks whether any coffee will exist, and existence takes the genitive as *nėra* does.
drills.explanation: The construction is the existential one: it asks whether there will be *any* coffee, and Lithuanian puts what may or may not exist into the genitive. *ar* is a particle and governs nothing (¶48).

drills.stem: Counting the present, the past and the future, how many **distinct sets of personal endings** must a learner know to conjugate any Lithuanian verb at this level?
drills.explanation: Three in the present (¶38), two in the past (¶89, ¶90), and one in the future — six. The future's single set is what makes it the easiest tense in the language, and it is why the dictionary needs only three principal parts and no fourth.

drills.title: Kitą savaitę
drills.passage: Kitą savaitę mes važiuosime prie jūros. Išvažiuosime penktadienį vakare ir grįšime sekmadienį. Ten bus šilta, bet vakarais bus vėsu. Aš nešiu didelį krepšį, o brolis neš maistą. Rūta sakė, kad ji nevažiuos — ji dirbs. „Kai grįšite, papasakosite“, — sakė ji. Po mėnesio mes visi būsime Vilniuje.
drills.translation: Next week we shall go to the seaside. We shall leave on Friday evening and return on Sunday. It will be warm there, but in the evenings it will be cool. I shall carry a large bag, and my brother will carry the food. Rūta said that she will not go — she will be working. "When you get back, you'll tell me about it," she said. In a month we shall all be in Vilnius.

questions.explanation: *grįšime sekmadienį* — the days of departure and return are both accusatives of time (¶83), naming single occasions.

questions.stem: Which future forms in the passage come from stems whose final consonant **merged** with the -s- marker?
questions.explanation: *grįž-* and *neš-* both absorb the marker. *dirb-* ends in b, which stands beside an s perfectly well, so *dirbs* keeps both consonants.

questions.stem: How many **negated** verbs does the passage contain?
questions.explanation: One: *nevažiuos*, Rūta's refusal. The negative is written onto the front of the verb as a single word (¶97), which is what makes it easy to overlook when counting.
